en: In the *Peṭakopadesa*, the section on the "Attainment of the Modes" (*Hārasampātabhūmi*):

Regarding those four meditations (*jhāna*), these are their factors (*aṅga*); the collection of those factors is their "factors" (*aṅgā*). This is the "ground of meditation" (*jhānabhūmi*). What is its distinction? Its distinction is this.
These are the requisites; by means of these is this attainment. This is the proximate cause for that attainment; by means of that proximate cause is this development.
This is the disadvantage of that development;
by means of that is this decline.
"Whose is the decline? refers to one who possesses that attainment through jhāna.
This distinction is made by reflecting upon it exactly as it has been described.
By means of that distinction, this is the gratification; for whom is that gratification? It is for the non-meditator and the meditator; [it belongs] to that non-meditator and meditator.
This skillful state, established in jhāna, reaches an unassailable condition through the power of jhāna.
For one established in the power of jhāna who has attained perfection, these factors of jhāna are cultivated as the first jhāna with unpolluted intention.

Joy (*pīti*) is a factor of the first jhāna precisely because it follows after that [intention]; and the other mental states associated with those factors are so called because they are thoroughly saturated by it.

Rapture (*pīti*) is a factor of the second jhāna by its nature as a jhāna-factor; furthermore, for one proceeding thus, the internal clarity (*ajjhattaṃ sampasādo*) accompanied by that jhāna-factor is a factor of the second jhāna due to the state of mental clarity and being saturated by it.
Rapture is a factor of the second jhāna; internal clarity is a factor of the second jhāna through the state of concentration (*samādhitā*). Rapture is a factor of the second jhāna.
One-pointedness of mind is a factor of absorption in the second jhāna; equanimity and contact are factors of absorption in the third jhāna, and happiness is its factor as well.

One-pointedness of mind is a factor of absorption in the fourth jhāna; equanimity that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant is a factor of absorption in the fourth jhāna; and equanimity-purity-of-mindfulness, which is the ground for focused application, is a factor of absorption in the fourth jhāna.
Purity of mindfulness, associated with the factors of jhāna across various levels of jhāna, and rapture as the unification of mind, is a factor of jhāna in the fourth jhāna.
In this context, what is the level of jhāna?
The level of jhāna in the first jhāna is that which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, and is followed by seclusion.
In the second jhāna stage, there is internal serenity free from applied and sustained thought, accompanied by the rapture born of that.
In the third jhāna stage, one is absorbed in blissful pleasure and possessed of rapture.
In the fourth jhāna stage, it is accompanied by the transcendence of pleasure and pain, and accompanied by the resolve [of equanimity].
The plane of jhāna in the first jhāna consists of those states accompanied by the immeasurables (appamāṇa) having beings as their object.
The plane of jhāna in the second jhāna consists of those states accompanied by the bases of mastery (abhibhū-āyatana) while still possessing the perception of form.
The plane of jhāna in the third jhāna consists of those states accompanied by the liberations (vimokkha).
The bodily formations accompanied by contemplation are the right ground for the fourth jhāna.
In this regard, what are the specific qualities of the jhāna?

Being quite secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, there is the transcendence of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) accompanied by mind and mental factors; this is a specific quality of the jhāna.

Perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by rapture, accompanied by joy, and accompanied by mindfulness—being without applied thought (*avitakka*) and without sustained thought (*avicāra*)—occur.
This is the distinction of the jhāna.
On the plane without applied thought, when there is indeed no sustained thought, acts of attention accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) occur, following after mindfulness.
And when mindfulness is present in accordance with that state, it becomes steady;
he enters and dwells in that plane—this is a distinction of jhāna.
Perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by the purity of mindfulness operate; he enters and dwells in that plane—this is a distinction of jhāna.

When perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of nothingness arise on the plane associated with the base of infinite consciousness, and one enters and dwells in that plane—this is the distinction of the jhāna.
The requisites for jhāna are as follows: the thought of renunciation is a requisite through its intention to dispel thoughts of sensual desire;
the thought of non-ill will is a requisite through its intention to dispel thoughts of ill will.
The equipment consisting of non-cruelty-thought is the intention to dispel cruelty-thought.
Guarding the doors of the sense-faculties and fewness of desires is the equipment for pure livelihood; dwelling in non-action is the equipment for the four meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
The equipment of the Path is the state of entering into attainment.
The equipment for the fruit is the attainment of jhāna through the production of jhāna.
As for the wholesome cause: that jhāna which proceeds toward arising, and from what does it arise? It arises from those who have attained renunciation.
The concentration on the cessation of objects arises as peaceful.
They arise without transgression.
They arise for the abandoning of the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy, and they arise for non-affliction;
indeed, it is with reference to that that they arise.
They arise for the sake of non-affliction.
This is the attainment of knowledge.
In this regard, what is the proximate cause?
Good friendship is a proximate cause for jhāna.
Association with the good is a proximate cause for jhāna.
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties is a proximate cause for jhāna.
Non-contentment with wholesome states is a proximate cause for jhāna.
Hearing the true Dhamma is a proximate cause for jhāna.
For one who is stirred by a stirring place, appropriate exertion is a proximate cause for jhāna.
This is the proximate cause for jhāna.
In this context, what is development?
It is the cultivation of loving-kindness, which is the development of thoughts of non-ill will.
The cultivation of compassion is the development of non-harming thoughts.
The cultivation of sympathetic joy is characterized by rapture, pleasure, and clear comprehension.
The cultivation of equanimity consists of both equanimity as looking on and equanimity as not looking on, as well as equanimity and thorough equanimity. The cultivation of the perception of foulness.
The painful practice with slow direct knowledge, which leads to the continuity of existence— this sixfold development,
when developed, cultivated, established, made a foundation, mastered, consolidated, and well undertaken, is called "development."
For one who develops [the path] in this way, this is the disadvantage:
in the first jhāna, this state is accompanied by volitional formations, unheard of [by the noble ones], and subject to taints.

If this state is this virtue, it is a proximate adversary; and this state—characterized by sensual desire, involving access and sustained application—is entirely grosser than the attainments, consisting of applied and sustained thought.
Therein, they disturb the mind, and the body becomes weary; when the body is weary, the mind is afflicted.
These are the disadvantages in the first jhāna for one who is incapable of directing [the mind] toward higher direct knowledges (abhiññā).
In the second jhāna, these are the disadvantages: this state is accompanied by the pervasion of rapture (pīti), yet the mind does not [remain] in its active manifestation.
This Dhamma is an approach that is not yet mastered; this Dhamma is a danger to those who approach it, and it is an adversary to mental grief.
In various instances, joy arises from the mastery of applications, yet this Dhamma is difficult to practice when one avoids the ground of instability and fear.
It is permeated by the suffering inherent in the four types of suffering, and by the suffering of faith, rather than the suffering of impediments.
And because of the suffering inherent in the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the suffering of illness, these are the disadvantages in the second jhāna.
In that regard, what are the disadvantages in the third jhāna?

Therein, for those who find gratification in that which is accompanied by equanimity and pleasure, this state—which has been turned away from equanimity and pleasure—becomes an object for their perception of permanence.
Happiness that brings suffering arises from the agitation of the mind; having fallen into pleasure and pain, it flows away.
And because it conforms to pleasure and pain, the mind becomes incapable of being sustained.
Regarding the direct knowledges and the realizations, all these states [are present] in the three meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) by way of the four kinds of suffering.
These are the disadvantages in the third jhāna: being permeated by fear, by the suffering of impediment, and by the suffering of higher knowledge.
In that regard, what are the disadvantages in the fourth jhāna?
Those states are the attainments of the base of nothingness; they are the attainments of the Dhamma. And upon this plane, various types of speculative views arise for foolish worldlings.
These jhānas are subtle compared to gross perceptions of form; they are always accompanied by the fraction and sub-fraction of the jhāna of boundless loving-kindness.
All four great requisites are difficult to fulfill, yet these jhānas have been fully accomplished through one another.
They arise depending [on these conditions].
Herein, these states that have arisen do not reach completion;
and these states fall away because their signs were not fully grasped.

These phenomena cease and are not grasped; the factors that would cease also cease. For these phenomena, the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and their signs do not arise, nor does the perception of the signs of the meditative absorptions disperse.
Although previously unattained, one becomes a meditator by way of the practice of meditation.
Through these disadvantages, this constitutes the decline of meditative absorption.

If, through lack of discernment regarding the attainment of cessation, while still possessing residual perceptions, perception and attention associated with the base of nothingness occur, he falls away from the attainment of cessation.

If, while possessing the perception of imperturbability and having entered the base of non-perception, attention associated with the base of nothingness occurs and he does not understand that plane, he falls away from it.
If, while having entered the base of nothingness, perception and attention associated with the base of infinite consciousness occur and he does not understand that plane, he falls away from it.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, [the perception] accompanied by the perception of form [is absent].
In detail... [and so on]... up to:
for the first jhāna, it should be stated as being accompanied by sensual perceptions.

For one who is distracted, he meditates with a stain; he meditates all around; he meditates while breaking [the object]; he does not recite; he meditates while exerting himself; and he meditates on something with which he is unfamiliar.
He meditates while racing too far; he meditates while despising [others]; he meditates on bodily formations that are not conducive to analytical knowledge;
he meditates without knowing the escape from the obsessions; he meditates overcome by the hindrances; he meditates while attending to the attainment of comfort.

The gratification of jhāna is the abandoning of the obsession with sensual lust; the gratification of jhāna is that while the factors of these states arise through causes rooted in sensual lust, they cease.
The higher jhānas are the gratification consisting in the abandoning of sensual desires, kamma, and defilements, as well as bliss and equanimity.
Such indeed is the gratification of jhāna within this worldly existence, which is oppressed by great crowds.
Through the abandoning of this jhāna, this lack of opportunity for enlightenment will vanish.

This is the benefit of this jhāna—the abandonment of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for those beings who have entered the beginningless cycle of rebirth—both in the world of conflict and in the world of non-conflict;
namely, that for one who meditates with a body not subject to fever, there is the gratification (*assāda*) of this jhāna.

Not grasping at the meditations of those who do not meditate on the non-defiled, one meditates on the meditation of the non-defiled meditator. Those words concerning the meditators on stains are directed toward their opposites.
In this regard, what is skill in meditation?
Skill in attainment is skill in meditation; skill in the distinctions of meditation is skill in meditation; skill in the intermediate stages of meditation is skill in meditation.
Skill in meditation, skill in emerging from attainment, skill in the individual nature of meditation,
skill in the disadvantage of meditation, skill in the escape from meditation, skill based on the fruit of meditation,
and the state of being non-prone to decline in the fruit of reflection regarding the meditation produced through the fruit of meditation.
And even while playing, one attains jhāna that partakes of distinction. Now, as for this [attainment]:

it consists of being carried along by existence (*bhavahāritā*), grasping the signless aspect of the object (*ārammaṇānimittaggāha*), the power of non-directing (*anabhinīhārabala*), one-pointedness of mind accompanied by movement toward the sign (*nimittāsu gatisahitā*), and non-sinking through the power of serenity (*samathabalena asaṁsīdana*) during the occurrence of jhāna, the path, and the fruit. Serenity (*samatha*) [is thus established].

For one who possesses concentration, the power of mindfulness is the basis for the preceding and succeeding signs of equanimity; and for one who exerts effort, it is the power of conventional designation regarding those insights that have arisen.
In this context, what is the perfection of meditation (jhānapāramitā)?

In the *Supāramitā-mettā* Sutta, where two truths— suffering and its origin— are indicated by way of the teaching’s terminology as "beings attached to sensual pleasures" and "beings stuck in the fetters of sensual pleasure," it is impossible that those who do not perceive the fault in things that lead to bondage will cross over the flood, according to the method of investigation.

“They shall not cross over”: there is this application and investigation as to what the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) of this is. “Attached to sensual pleasures” refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure; that is the proximate cause of craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
“Not seeing the fault in the fetters” is the proximate cause of ignorance (*avijjā*), for those who are attached to the bonds of the fetters can never cross over the vast and great flood.
“The proximate cause of clinging (*upādāna*): “attached to sensual pleasures”—sensual pleasures are twofold: [sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements].

There are sensual desires as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual desires as defilements (*kilesakāma*). Therein, sensual desires as defilements consist of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*); those joined with craving for sense-pleasures become, by way of their characteristic, craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). [This occurs] when they do not see the fault in the fetter (*saṁyojana*).
What is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for that desire and lust (*chandarāga*) therein?
It is pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*) and two faculties (*indriya*).
The faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy.
Thus, when pleasant feeling is grasped, all three types of feeling are grasped.
When the aggregate of feeling is grasped, all five aggregates are grasped.
Visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are included; when the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*) are included, all six external sense bases (*bāhirāyatana*) are thereby included.

Among the internal and external sense bases, that which is mindful is called the "conveying of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*). In this context, one who dwells with coarse defilements does not become free from passion toward those that are subtler than them.
Therein, the external fetter is "mine," while the internal fetter is "I."
In this regard, what is the Blessed One’s intention?
"Those who desire to cross the flood shall dwell contemplating the danger in phenomena that fetter"—this is the Blessed One’s intention here.

Regarding the phrase "clinging to sensual pleasures," these four aspects—those things to which beings cling, the means by which they cling, and those [beings] who cling—are all included within the modes of interpretation (*hāra*).
In this context, what are the three perversions and their respective foundations?
For the perversion of mind, the perversion of view, and the perversion of perception, the three perversions have the three unwholesome roots as their foundation.
The three unwholesome roots are the foundation for kamma that produces inferior or superior results.
And the fault of the four kinds of clinging is seen as an unwholesome root;
it is the proximate cause for performing inferior or superior deeds,
such as when one grants safety to a mother, a father, or some other eminent bhikkhu.
In that situation, another might act wrongly through body or speech.

Therein, he who, having taken up a state of ill will toward them, protects, shields, and guards those noble ones—giving them fearlessness—and then acts wrongly toward those very ones for whom fearlessness has been granted; [that is what is meant].
Therein, one who takes up ill will performs action born of hatred.
That which therein is unwholesome is a hindrance to the faculties; that which is their fearlessness is perception from the right side—this is the sublime cause.
Furthermore, wrong practice therein is this ill will, which is the action of a base person: greed and delusion.

And these words regarding the hindrances refer to those four types of clinging; by means of those four types of clinging, whatever woman or man clings, their five aggregates are themselves that clinging.
This is both suffering and its origin; this is the mode of teaching.
In this regard, those who do not proceed toward sense pleasures proceed by contemplating the danger [in them].
Thus, the desire to emerge from that element of sensual desire is called the will for renunciation (*nekkhammacchanda*).
Whatever therein purifies even a little of the unconditioned—that is the will for non-ill-will (*abyāpādacchanda*).
Whatever one harms, that is the intention to harm.
Thus, there are three intentions directed toward renunciation:
the intention for renunciation, the intention for non-ill will, and the intention for non-harming.
Therein, the desire for renunciation is non-greed;
the desire for non-ill will is non-hatred;
the desire for non-cruelty is non-delusion.
These three roots of the wholesome, when directed toward the welfare of others in the eight favorable circumstances, lead to the cessation of those very four kinds of clinging.
Alternatively, if one should perform karma that is either dark or bright, they lead to the diminution of its result.
This karma—which is neither dark nor bright—leads to the exhaustion of karma.
In this context, the cessation of the three unwholesome roots is *nirodha* (cessation).
That very path is the *paṭipadā* (practice) therein. These two truths and these four truths constitute the method of "turning" (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*).
Regarding "clinging to sense-pleasures," those who are trainees (*sekkhā*) cling in only one way.
Those who are worldlings are attached to beings in two ways; this question regarding them should be stated as one to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajjavyākaraṇīya*).
Although a stream-enterer may be attached to enjoyment, he is not attached through dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*), for he exerts himself toward diminution and not toward accumulation.
Indeed, it is the trainee (*sekha*) who enjoys sense pleasures by way of defilement.
But the worldling indulges in sensual pleasures arising from the defilements.
In that regard, as for those beings who are attached to sensual pleasures, the question "Will they cross over the four floods? is to be answered by analysis; this is the analysis (*vibhatti*).
As for the reversal (*parivattana*): "Those who neither cling to sensual pleasures nor are bound by fetters, they will cross over the vast and great flood."
This is the opposite of the sutta.
As for the synonyms: one who is attached to sensual pleasures, and whatever excellence there is in those sensual pleasures—one is attached to that.
Also, regarding the things that are the nutriment of sensual pleasures—one is attached to that.
In this regard, these are synonyms for sensual pleasures: ripening, dust, a dart, a boil, a plague, and a calamity.
Or whatever other synonyms there may be, in that context "being" (*satta*) is a synonym. [Synonyms for one who is bound] include:
a being, one bound, infatuated, clinging, attached, obsessed with sensual pleasures, not liberated from them, and one who dwells frequently therein.
Or whatever other synonyms there may be—this is what is called a synonym (*vevacana*).
"Mind" (*citta*) is a synonym for that which is designated by the designation of the practice of sensual desire and the designation of the domain of the defilements.
Or whatever other [terms] there may be, such as "a being" (*satta*) or "one who dwells frequently therein."
These are described by way of the description of indulgence in sensual pleasures; they are described by way of the description of the domain of defilements;
formations are described by way of the description of fetters; clinging is described by way of the description of causes; and the person is described by way of the description of diversity.
"Entry" (otaraṇa) means that by means of this [formula], dependent origination is both suffering and its origin.

Those defilements, those formations, and those fetters which are included within the aggregate of formations among the five aggregates; those unwholesome phenomena among the bases of phenomena; and among the faculties, the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy—this is "entry by way of the faculties.
"Purification" (sodhana) means "to such an extent."
That very undertaking is to be demonstrated as the meaning of the sutta. Regarding "the foundation":
these phenomena exist as being designated by way of unity; they exist as being designated by way of diversity.
Those perceptions that are external sensual pleasures are designated by way of diversity.
"Beings attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure" is a designation for the diversity of obsessions and perversions; may they cross the flood.
"Vast and great" is a designation for ignorance as a single unity.
"Requisite": what is its cause, what is its condition?
It is a condition by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
And improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is a condition by way of being a support-condition (*sannissaya-paccaya*).
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is a condition by way of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
The underlying tendency to lust (*rāgānusaya*) is a condition by way of the relation of cause (*hetupaccayatā*).
This is the cause; this is the condition.

As for the application of the condition: the attachment and lust for sense pleasures—the thought that beings therein are "well-gone" or "beautiful"—these are volitional formations consisting of demerit (*apuññamaya-saṅkhāra*) within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
What is their condition?
Ignorance is their condition.
Of what are they the condition?
With consciousness as condition.
Thus, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness, and so on up to aging and death. In this way there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering. This concludes one discourse.
The *Pañcanīvaraṇika Sutta* should be composed.
In that context, what is called the "nourishment of teaching"?
Covetousness, ill will, and restlessness—these are craving (*taṇhā*).
That which is sloth and torpor, that which is remorse, and that which is doubt—this is [the category of] view.

However, as for the unwieldiness of the body, although it is indeed torpor, it is not a defilement by virtue of being a defilement in its own nature; thus, both the sinking of the mind and the unwieldiness of the body are secondary defilements (pakkhopakileso), but not defilements in their own nature.

In this context, weariness accumulated through self-perception and remorse accumulated through anxiety are the lethargy that is the sinking of the mind; thus, these five hindrances consist of four hindrances that are defilements by their very nature (*sabhāva-kilesa*), while lethargy-and-drowsiness is a secondary defilement belonging to the side of the hindrances.

Just as the four taints (*āsava*) are "taints" by virtue of being taints by their very nature, rather than being taints because they taint the mind, so too [the hindrances] are taints by virtue of their own nature.
They are "with taints" (sāsava) by virtue of being taints themselves.
Alternatively, one might say: those taints with which they are either associated or dissociated—those very taints should be called "with taints" or "without taints.
In this regard, what is the investigation?
Covetousness consists of craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for existence;

or whatever else has become an object of attachment, which is subject to taints and covetous. When one practices loving-kindness meditation toward such a person, whoever acts for their harm—thinking, "He has acted, he will act," or "He is acting"—therein gives rise to ill will.
In this way, the nine grounds for resentment are to be applied. For one who thus contemplates ill will, the defilement consists of burning fever, bodily exhaustion, unworkability, and drowsiness.
For one who contemplates the mind, there is despondency due to resistance; this is sloth and torpor.
In that regard, the lack of settlement of a legal issue is restlessness.
"What is this that I have done?"—this is remorse (*kukkucca*).
"What is this, and how is it?"—this is investigation, which is doubt (*vicikicchā*).
In that regard, where both ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) exist, this is obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
There is an obstruction, a hindrance, a covering, and a defilement; this is the proximate cause for the obsession of sensual desire.
Ill will is the proximate cause for the obsession of ill will.
Sloth and torpor are the proximate cause for the obsession of sloth and torpor.
Restlessness and remorse are the proximate cause for the obsession of ignorance.
Doubt is the proximate cause for the obsession of doubt.
The obsession of sensual lust is the proximate cause for the fetter of underlying tendency.
The obsession with ill will is the proximate cause for the fetter of aversion.
The obsession with sloth and torpor is the proximate cause for the fetter of conceit.
Both the obsession with ignorance and the obsession with doubt are the proximate causes for the fetter of views.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra)?
When "obsession by sensual lust" is mentioned, all obsessions are thereby mentioned.
When "fetters" are mentioned, all fetters are thereby mentioned.
This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (*catubyūha-hāra*)?
These five hindrances are the opposite of the meditative absorptions; they are the origin of suffering.
That which is the fruit is suffering.
In that regard, the thought of renunciation is the antidote to sensual desire;
the thought of non-ill will is the antidote to ill will.
Non-cruelty-thought is the antidote to three hindrances.
Thus, these are the three types of thought.
The thought of renunciation belongs to the aggregate of concentration.
Thought of non-ill will pertains to the aggregate of virtue;
thought of non-cruelty pertains to the aggregate of wisdom.
These are the three aggregates.
The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the abandoning of the hindrances.
That which is the abandoning of the hindrances is cessation.
These are the Four Truths.
This is the fourfold method of analysis (*catubyūha-hāra*).
In this regard, what is the method of turning back (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*)?
The five hindrances become ten.
Whatever one is lustful toward internally, that too is an hindrance;
whatever one is lustful toward externally, that too is an hindrance. Thus, up to doubt—these are the ten hindrances.
Internally and externally, these defilements constitute these two fetters: the internal fetter and the external fetter.
In this context, "I" refers to the internal, and "mine" refers to the external.
The view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is internal, while the sixty-one types of speculative views are external.
That which is lustful desire for forms internally is being undetached from passion and undetached from desire.
Thus, up to consciousness, this is internal craving.
That which is attachment to the six external bases and to the three realms of existence, this is external craving.
These two truths are the fetters and the things that are subject to fettering.
In this context, regarding the phenomena that are fetters: the contemplation of disenchantment is the path;
the abandoning of the fetters is cessation.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Conversion.
In this context, what is the method of analysis?
"Fetter" is not unilaterally [the case].
The fetter of conceit that belongs to the category of views does not abandon [its object] unilaterally; it does not abandon that which is not based on views or conceit.
Whatever conceit regarding the five higher fetters there may be, even if it belongs to the side of [wrong] view, it does not lead to the abandoning of the lower fetters.
And as for this "I-making," it is not cast aside; rather, he thinks thus: [this is mine].

"May I at some time realize for myself that peaceful state, enter into it, and dwell therein—that peaceful state which the Noble Ones will realize, enter, and dwell in"—this is covetousness, yet it is not an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
However, there is the case where even an Arahant falls into bodily defilement and sloth; this is not an hindrance for him, yet "sloth and torpor are an hindrance.
This is not so categorically.
This is the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāra*).
As for the Mode of Reversal (*parivattanā*): the five hindrances are abandoned by means of the five-factored jhāna.
This is their opposite. One should not infer otherwise that "this hindrance has been abandoned by such-and-such a person"; rather, it is ultimately internal. This is the Mode of Reversal.
In this context, what are the synonyms?
Sensual desire, lustful craving, affection, and attachment—these are synonyms.
Hindrance, covering, defilement, and obsession—these are synonyms.

“Description” means: ignorance is described by way of the description of its function; ill will is described by way of the description of distraction; sloth and torpor are described by way of the description of non-eradication.
Thus, all these five hindrances in this sutta are described by way of the description of distraction.
In this regard, what is the entry?
These five hindrances, ignorance, and craving: therein, the hindrances have ignorance as their root.

That which is craving is these volitional formations; these two phenomena have ignorance as their condition. These two phenomena are included within the aggregate of volitional formations among the five aggregates;
they are the base of mental phenomena among the bases; they are the mental-phenomena element among the elements; and this is the footing for these phenomena among the faculties.
[The faculties] of pleasure, mental joy, femininity, and masculinity.
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification?
This discourse was set forth concerning this [subject], and that meaning has been expressed by these five terms.
In this context, sensual desire, ill will, and doubt are not designated as a unity; "sensual pleasures" are also not designated as a unity, but rather they are designated as a diversity.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Basis (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*).
In this context, what is the Mode of Requisites (*parikkhāra*)?
For sensual desire, unwise attention is the condition consisting of a beautiful object,
and the sign of beauty is the cause.
For ill will, unwise attention and the grounds for resentment are the conditions.
The underlying tendency to aversion is the cause.
The withdrawal from sloth and torpor is the condition;
for their occurrence, fatigue and agitation are the causes.
For restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*), the condition is an object that is attractive, desirable, and gratifying to the faculties, as well as incomplete knowledge;
the cause is sensual perception (*kāmasaññā*) and the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*).
For doubt (*vicikicchā*), the ninefold conceit is the object and the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) is the condition.
The underlying tendency to doubt is the cause.
These five phenomena arise with a cause and with conditions.
In this regard, what is the method of coordination?
These five hindrances, these four taints, these abscesses, these arrows, and these clingings—all these are external phenomena.
Among them, it is designated as a "discourse dealing with defilement.
This is the Mode of Conveying Coordination.
The discourse dealing with the side of defilement has been demonstrated.
The verse beginning with "Phenomena are preceded by the mind"—
in that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying the Teaching?

In this sutta, what is the meaning? By the analysis of the aggregates (*khandhavavatthāna*), it teaches the aggregate of consciousness; by the analysis of the elements (*dhātuvavatthāna*), the mind-consciousness element; by the analysis of the bases (*āyatanavavatthāna*), the mind base; and by the analysis of the faculties (*indriyavavatthāna*), the mind faculty.

What are its preceding factors? In brief, six factors are the preceding factors: the roots of the wholesome and the roots of the unwholesome. In this sutta, the root of the wholesome is taught as being signless (*animitta*).
In this context, what are the phenomena preceded by the mind?
The mind is their precursor; just as a king is the precursor of his army, even so are phenomena preceded by the mind.
In that regard, there are three kinds of precursors: the desire for renunciation, the desire for non-ill will, and the desire for non-harming.
Non-greed is preceded by the aspiration for renunciation;
non-hatred is preceded by the aspiration for non-ill will;
non-delusion is preceded by the aspiration for non-cruelty.
In this context, "mind is foremost" (*manoseṭṭha*) means that these phenomena have surged forth by means of the mind, or they are fashioned by the mind.
Mind is the foremost among these phenomena; mind is the eldest among these phenomena; mind exercises sovereignty over these phenomena—thus, "mind is foremost.
"Mind-swift" (*manojava*) means wherever the mind goes.
In this context, these states go by means of the mind, thus they are "mind-swift" (*manojavā*).

Just as the wind goes swiftly, or any other thing that goes swiftly is called "wind-swift" (*vātajava*) or "bird-swift" (*pakkhigāmika*), even so these states go as they arise together with the mind; because these states go therein, they are "mind-swift."
These are threefold when brought about by desire: non-turbidity and intention.
And sevenfold is bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct; these are the ten courses of wholesome action (*daśa kuśalakarmapathāḥ*).
Therein, "if with a mind serene" refers to mental action.
"Speaks or utters" refers to verbal action;
"does or performs" refers to bodily action.
By these [terms], in this sutta, the ten courses of wholesome action, even when at their highest, are the supreme forms of virtue and conduct.
Thus, in the context of turning away from existence, it becomes a discourse pertaining to the portion of spiritual cultivation for the sake of departing from the world.
This is the teaching.
In this regard, what is the method of analysis?
"States are preceded by mind": this refers to the roots of wholesomeness and the eight factors of rightness;
this is the Sutta.
As for the "Yutti" (logical connection): whatever is the result of the ten wholesome courses of action is to be experienced as pleasant, being comprised within non-ill-will.
The phrase "like a shadow that never departs" refers to the logical connection (yutti) that it follows [the mind].
"Its proximate cause" (padaṭṭhāna) means it is the proximate cause for the eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra).
Regarding the statement "states are preceded by the mind," these states are the proximate cause for the entire side of the wholesome (kusala-pakkha).
"With a mind serene" refers to that serenity of the mind; this is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
"Speaks" is the proximate cause for right speech (*sammāvācā*).
"Acts" is the proximate cause for both right action (*sammākammanta*) and right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).

Regarding the characteristic: "These states have mindfulness as their forerunner"—these have feeling as their forerunner, these have perception as their forerunner, and these have volitional formations as their forerunner.
Whatever states are co-nascent, they all have these states as their forerunner.
"Then happiness follows after him"—mental joy (*somanassa*) follows after him, and whatever shadow of exquisite pleasure there is at that time, that happiness also follows after him.
In this context, what is the fourfold method of analysis (catubyūha-hāra)?
The verse beginning with "Mind precedes" is not a statement consisting of a single [term] and so forth.
For what reason?
All these groups of consciousness of the skin—what is the Blessed One’s intention here?
"Those who desire happiness clarify their minds"—this is the Blessed One’s intention in this sutta.
The meaning has already been explained.
For those which are the roots of the wholesome, they are the cause by virtue of having eight benefits; this is the Eightfold Path.
There are ten points which are the causes for teaching and the conditions for teaching, as well as the exposition.

In that regard, when one conceives of name-and-form together with suffering as the truth of consciousness, the root of the wholesome is abandoned through that factor; this is the origin within the plane of the unabandoned.
That which is their abandoning is cessation.
These are the four truths.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Conversion.
“Analysis” means:
“Phenomena are preceded by the mind,
led by the mind, and made of the mind.”
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows that person.
"Like a shadow that never departs"—this is not necessarily the case for a recluse or a brahmin.

Or, when one with wrong view gladdens the mind in his own teaching and speaks and explains with that gladdened mind, happiness does not follow him, nor does it accompany him like a shadow; rather, suffering alone follows him.
"Just as the wheel follows the foot of one who draws it"—this is the answer to be given after analysis (*vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya*).

"If with a confident mind, bodily action and verbal action are to be experienced as pleasant": when proceeding rightly they are to be experienced as pleasant, but when proceeding wrongly they are to be experienced as painful; this is the analysis (*vibhatti*).
In this regard, what is the method of reversal (*parivattano hāro*)?
"Mind precedes all mental states": whatever one speaks or does with a corrupted mind brings suffering in its wake—these two very suttas were spoken, and this is their antidote.
As for synonyms: what is called *mano*, *citta*, *viññāṇa*, *manindriya*, and *manoviññāṇadhātu*.
As for the designation (*paññatti*): in the phrase "mind precedes all mental states," this *mano* is designated by some form of designation.
“Dhammas” is designated by way of the designation of the wholesome courses of action.
“Mind is chief” is designated by way of a distinguished designation.
“Swift as the mind” is designated by way of a simultaneous designation.
“Mind” is described by way of the description of renunciation.
“If with a serene mind” is described by way of the description of the faculty of faith.
“If with a serene mind” is described by way of the description of the second jhāna, which has undisturbed intention as its companion.
"With a mind full of confidence" is formulated as the designation for the opposite of those lacking faith.
"He speaks" is formulated as the designation for right speech.
"He acts" is formulated as the designation for right action.
"Then happiness follows him"—this refers to the concentration of jhāna.
Among the faculties, it is the mind-faculty;
in dependent origination, it is consciousness.
"States are preceded by mind": this refers to loving-kindness (*mettā*) and mental pliancy (*mudutā*). Among the jhānas, they are included in the second and third jhānas.
Among the aggregates (*khandha*), they are comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Among the elements (*dhātu*), they are the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*); among the bases (*āyatana*), they are the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
That which is wholesome—the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy—is the proximate cause.

For these dependently arisen phenomena, conditioned by contact, there is contact to be experienced as pleasant; pleasant feeling; mental joy among the mental explorations; and the six types of renunciation-based mental joy among the first thirty-six [mental explorations].
Thus is this Mode of Conveying the Entryway.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification (sodhana-hāra)?
It is that meaning with reference to which this discourse was spoken;
that meaning is established, for it is with reference to this meaning that the discourse was spoken.
This is the Mode of Conveying Purification.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Determination?
“Mind precedes all phenomena” is a designation by synonym, not a designation of identity.
“Dhammas” is not a designation of synonyms used collectively.
“With a serene mind”: that serenity is twofold, consisting of internal non-suppression of ill will and external confidence (*okappanā*).
That internal serenity is twofold.
The confidence of eradication and the confidence of suppression [counteract] the obsession of ill will.
There is affliction, not the confidence of the root, or even that which has arisen as a root.
Confidence is accompanied by ill will through affliction.

"Then happiness follows him": this happiness is both bodily and mental; it includes the happiness of being separated from the unloved, the happiness of being united with the loved, the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of worldlings, and the mental happiness of the joy factor of enlightenment (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
That which one feels as happiness when the body is tranquil is bodily happiness, while the factors of enlightenment are mental happiness.

Furthermore, that happiness which one feels when the body is tranquil, as well as its basis (*padatthāna*), is designated as such according to what has been stated; it is not adhered to by wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*).
"It follows" refers to absorption; yet this [absorption] does not follow as something already attained.
This sutta should be resolved in two ways:
by way of the cause, which is the mind that is confident, and by way of the result, which is that which is to be experienced as suffering.
"Requisites," said the Blessed One, "are when the Blessed One enters the city of Rājagaha with a community of five hundred bhikkhus.
There, a certain person serves the Blessed One; faith arises in him, and he is one who has previously practiced the roots of wholesome merit.
He tells others, speaking these words: 'It is a gain for those whose residence the Blessed One enters; if it were so for us as well, we too would obtain serene confidence in the Blessed One.'"
Having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and saying, “Homage to the Blessed One! Homage to the Blessed One! he stood to one side without ill will.
Immediately thereafter, the Blessed One spoke this discourse: “Phenomena are preceded by the mind.
The entire discourse that one speaks to others is vocal action (*vācākamma*).
That which is the bowing of the palms in añjali is bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
That which is mental confidence (*manopasāda*) is mental action (*manokamma*).
Therein, that which one proclaims and speaks in praise of others is verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
"Whosever house the Blessed One visits"— for all of that,
non-greed is the root of the wholesome.
"Whoever has a mind of loving-kindness toward the Blessed One"— for that, non-hatred is the root of the wholesome.
In that he bows with palms joined and restrains his pride, non-delusion as a root of the wholesome becomes manifest to him.
That he acquires sublime wisdom is his abandonment of the perversion of view.
That there is likewise restraint is his abandonment of the perversion of perception.
That which is the clarity of the mind is the abandoning of its cognitive distortions (*cittavipallāsa*); thus, the suppression-abandoning of unwholesome distortions is the condition.
The three wholesome roots—that intention which is an undisturbed state of mind—is called "attention" (*manasikāra*).

That which is the suppression by means of the defilements—namely, the distortions together with their objects as the condition for having conditions, and the wholesome roots as the condition for being manifest—and that attention arising through this cause and this condition, is the mind that has arisen.
In this context, that consciousness which proceeds with the Buddha as its object is "recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, when one brings to mind the qualities of the Blessed One, this constitutes his "recollection of the Dhamma.
In this regard, mindfulness and clear comprehension are the cause, and this [recollection] is the condition.
Speech and wisdom are the cause; applied thought and sustained thought are the condition.

Bodily formations are called the formative activity of karma; they are either the cause or the non-condition. They are the cause for the accumulation of karma to be experienced as pleasure, and they are the condition for that karma.
In this context, what is the method of coordination?
"By means of the mind alone, one is serene; by means of the mind alone, one is clear here. Furthermore, beings are liberated through the purification of the mind;
thus, beings are preceded by the mind. When the mind is serene, volition also becomes characterized by that serenity of the mind.
This is the repelling of volitions through serenity, and this is the body of that serenity. And he who is serene through serenity undertakes perceptions through serenity."

And this is its non-erroneous [nature]. It is fivefold: suppression, tranquility of the body, confidence itself, that which is dependent on the mind, and the mind itself, which was already confident previously.
This is the application.
In this way, there is confidence even in the five [aggregates].
When it is said, "Then happiness follows after him," what does the Blessed One point to?
For it is not the reality of a self that follows as the result of that karma.
The means follows it when joy arises conditioned by pleasure; non-remorse also follows.
This is the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropano hāro*).
The Discourse to Mahānāma the Sakyan.
And if at that time one should die unmindful and lacking clear comprehension, one is reborn in the realm of sense-desires.

"Unmindful but concentrated": "Do not fear, Mahānāma," [he said]. This should be explained in detail: "That mind which for a long time has been cultivated by faith, cultivated by virtue, and cultivated by learning and generosity.
And what does he show by means of generosity and wisdom?
That which is faith is clarity of mind.
That which is free from turbidity in its intention is faith.
For what reason?
It has the characteristic of being untroubled.
For faith has the characteristic of being untroubled.
Others say it has the characteristic of reaching the culmination of the purification of qualities; and others say that faith has the characteristic of receiving what is spoken.
Another method: if one resolves regarding oneself thus, "I know nothing at all; this is my state of non-knowing there, permitted by that," this is faith (*saddhā*).
Another method: it is the contemplation of the danger in the sixty-one types of speculative views as impermanent, suffering, and non-self (*anattā*).
And by that, it is "seen" in the sense that, as when one sees water with the eye in a deep well but does not reach it with the body,
so too his view comes about through noble reflective acceptance, yet it is not yet realized.
This is called faith.

And that is mundane. Another method is acceptable: for one who has become an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), there are twenty [fetters]. What is it that is not an adherence dependent on the view of self-identity (*sakkāya*)?
This is not a single thing; rather, the perception of a "method" is according to reality. Indeed, through the five faculties that are mild, they are abandoned by the path of vision (*dassanamagga*).
The defilements abandoned by vision—this is faith.
On this plane, it is said to be fulfilled as a factor of stream-entry.
On that very same plane, it is said that the Noble Ones maintain the virtue of one in training (sekkha-sīla).
On that very plane, soft wisdom is called the faculty of wisdom.
On that very plane, the lack of concern for the aggregates is generosity (*cāga*).
Therefore, faith should be demonstrated by means of the foundation of generosity.
For one who possesses excessive pride, that view is indeed perverted, lacking faith; it is undertaken while being negligent regarding the requisites for the journey.

In this regard, the faculty of faith consists in the relinquishing of what is burning through desire; the foundation of generosity does not exist there, but rather the foundation of wisdom through the faculty of wisdom, and the foundation of peace through virtue.
These four qualities—faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom—thoroughly cultivate virtue.
Therein, one crosses the flood by means of faith. That which is virtue is diligence;
that which is generosity is the work of wisdom.
That which is wisdom is the faculty of wisdom; therein,
that which is the faculty of faith is included within the three kinds of verified confidence,
and that which is virtue is included within the faculties of faith.
That which is generosity is found in the four meditative absorptions;
that which is wisdom is found in the truths, and mindfulness leads everywhere.
For that trainee, there is a blessed radiance and a blessed future destiny.

For one who has forgotten mindfulness while performing virtuous conduct, those faculties or that root of merit do not become the maturation of kamma due to that forgetfulness of mindfulness regarding the body.
This is the explanation of the meaning of that triad.
In that context, faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom are the four qualities.
That which is faith and that which is wisdom—this is good conduct of mind.
That which is virtue—this is good conduct of body and speech.
And that which is generosity—this is the mental state of non-greed as good conduct.
Thus, when the mind is grasped, the five aggregates are grasped.
By means of these phenomena, this good conduct and this Noble Truth of Suffering constitute the footing for the Path.
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Investigation?
And what is faith, and what is virtue?
What does that accomplish?
By means of that faith, one recollects the Blessed One: "Even when encountering a rutting elephant, there are dogs for him."

One does not practice everything through virtue, whether by body or by speech; there is a state where one becomes confident, being without remorse, and wisdom establishes what has been prescribed for him.
In that state of unbroken virtue, no unwholesome mind accompanied by delusion or associated with wrong view arises in him. This is the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicaya-hāra*).
"Those who speak of the Dhamma will be fortunate"—this is a logical connection.
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying the Footings?
That mind which has been cultivated for a long time through faith, virtue, generosity, wisdom, and concentration is the footing for the first jhāna.
The faith that he possesses, with its unclouded intention, is the proximate cause for the second jhāna.
The three kinds of verified confidence and the virtue that is dear to the noble ones are the proximate cause for the aggregate of virtue.
The wisdom that he possesses is the proximate cause for the aggregate of wisdom.
These qualities and this mind are the proximate cause for one-pointed concentration.
Faith is the proximate cause for the faculty of faith.
Generosity is the proximate cause for the faculty of concentration.
Wisdom is the proximate cause for the faculty of wisdom.
Both faith and wisdom are the proximate causes for insight.
Virtue and generosity are the proximate causes for serenity.
Faith and wisdom are the footing for the liberation of wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.
Virtue and generosity are the footing for the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust.
In this context, what is the method of characteristics?
When consciousness is mentioned as being developed through faith and mindfulness, all five aggregates are thereby mentioned.
When faith is spoken of, all seven kinds of wealth are spoken of: the wealth of faith...
[and so on] ...When the aggregate of virtue is mentioned, the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom are also mentioned.
It is impossible that the mind which has been cultivated for a long time would not continue to follow [the practitioner] in the final period;
such a case does not exist. In that regard, perception also continues to follow it, and those states of a similar nature likewise continue to follow it.

The attention consisting in the contemplation of perception of forms and volition regarding forms, and likewise for the six sense bases and the body of consciousness—this is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇo hāro*).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (*catubyūho hāro*)?
Herein, what is the Blessed One’s intention in this discourse?
Those who might desire a fortunate rebirth and a fortunate future existence will attend to faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom; this is the intended meaning.
And as for those other beings who do not apply themselves in the presence of the Tathāgata, they will die without regret after hearing this Dhamma; this is the intended meaning.
In this regard, what is the method of conversion (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*)?
In this case as well, these four qualities—faith and wisdom—destroy lack of faith and ignorance;
while virtue and generosity destroy craving and hatred.
Thus, his two roots are abandoned.
It turns back suffering; on the plane where [defilements] have not yet been abandoned, there are two roots and the five aggregates.
There are two Noble Truths, as well as serenity and insight.
It is the abandoning of the two roots.
These two truths are cessation and the path.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Conversion (āvaṭṭa-hāra).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Analysis (vibhatti)?
As for that mind which is permeated by faith...

even if it belongs to an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), its destiny will be auspicious; however, one cannot say with certainty that its kamma will ripen in this very life, as it may ripen in another future turn of existence.

Or, whatever past [kamma] has manifested for the sake of ripening, these [present factors] are its conditions. As it is said in the *Mahākammavibhaṅga*: "Therefore, this exposition regarding those who live according to the Dhamma, concerning their 'auspicious destiny,' is to be explained by way of analysis."
In this context, what is the reversal (*parivattanā*)?
Lack of faith, immorality, stinginess, and lack of wisdom—whatever is abandoned by means of their opposites: this is the reversal.
In this context, what is the synonym (*vevacana*)?
That mind which has been cultivated for a long time—the mind, the mental consciousness...
[and so on] ...that which is the power of faith, the faculty of faith; that which is virtue, that is good conduct; restraint, regulation, self-control, and wholesomeness—these are its synonyms.
That which is generosity is relinquishment, non-greed, surrender, and the sphere of giving.
That which is wisdom is described as wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, and the power of wisdom.
In this context, what is description?
It is that mind which, as a seed, is described by means of description.
Cultivation is described by means of the description of latent tendency.
Faith is described by means of the description of clarity.
Virtue is described by means of the description of good conduct.
Generosity is designated by way of the designation of meritorious action;
wisdom is designated by way of the designation of investigation.
These three qualities—faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom—reach complete purity for one possessed of wisdom.
In this regard, what is the method of entry?
That which is consciousness is, among the aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness; among the elements, the mind-consciousness element; among the bases, the mind base.
Those four states are included within the aggregate of formations among the aggregates … [and so on] …
Regarding the elements and the sense bases:
therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification?
This speech of the Blessed One, when questioned by Mahānāma the Sakyan, has all been applied accordingly.
In this context, what is the determination?
This mind is designated by way of diversity as being "unperfumed" by unwholesome states of consciousness or "perfumed" by them;
furthermore, regarding those which are perfumed, it is designated there with reference to others as well—all these are four phenomena.
It is described by way of unity.

"A fortunate livelihood" means that for those who enjoy sensual pleasures, as well as for those in the form realm, the formless realm, and among humans—all these constitute a fortunate livelihood; this is what is described by that discourse. This is description (*paññatti*).
In this context, what is equipment (*parikkhāra*)?
The faculties are conditions for the mind by way of predominance-conditionality;
attention is a condition by way of root-conditionality.
Worldly wisdom is a condition for faith by way of root-conditionality.
Appropriate attention is the condition;
dwelling in a suitable locality is the condition for virtue;
and right aspiration for oneself is the cause.
Non-greed is the cause of generosity.
Non-remorse is both its cause and its condition.
Wisdom, the voice of another, and wise attention directed inwardly are its cause and its condition.
In this context, what is the application?
That mind which has been cultivated for a long time—its mental concomitants have also been cultivated.
Herein, all phenomena have been cultivated; auspicious will be its radiance, and auspicious its rebirth and future destiny.
Thus, whatever human enjoyments and luxuries there may be, they are all merely a goodly hire; this is the application (*samāropana*).
Regarding the verse: "Above, below, and everywhere, free from passion"—therein, what is meant by "above"?
That which will be hereafter is "above" (*uddha*).
"Below" (*adho*) refers to that which has been transcended and is past; this is what was called "above" in the *Apadāna* collection.

Therein, by means of the past, there is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) of those who speculate about the prior limit (*pubbantākappika*), and for some, the view regarding the subsequent limit (*aparantadiṭṭhi*). For those speculators who have spoken [of annihilation], there is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). These views—both the annihilationist view and the eternalist view—are [thus addressed].
In this regard, among these fifteen terms, the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) pertains to eternalism as part of the embodiment-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
When it is said: "Form belongs to my self," "Form is in my self," or "My self is in form," one is burning with wisdom.
As for the view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi), those five hundred terms pertain to annihilation.
They view it thus: "The soul is the same as the body. Such a fourfold personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)—which holds "form is my self"—is characterized by both annihilationism and eternalism.
Thus, among the five aggregates, fifteen positions of this twenty-based view pertain to the past.
Five positions of the eternalist view pertain to the future, and [five] of the annihilationist view.

In this context, one who views [the self] as "I am this" regards form as the self; he is an annihilationist (ucchedavādī) who regards the self as possessing form, form as being in the self, or the self as being in form.
Thus he sees both the view of annihilation and the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), for he harks back to the self from the perspective of the past.
“He does not regard [anything] as ‘This I am.
Thus his taints of views come to be abandoned.
Whatever has been specified by this or that description regarding the three times—the past, the future, and the present—and above, below, and everywhere...”

"One free from lust does not contemplate 'I am'"—by this door, by this application, and by this means, this stage of vision and the fruit of stream-entry constitute that noble application. Through the non-existence of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no further becoming;
whatever noble application there may be for further becoming consists of either the five faculties in their weak or middling states.
Or rather, all these supreme [qualities] lead to the abandonment of renewed existence.
"I" refers to the flood of views, the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, and the flood of ignorance; thus they are specific.
Therein, by way of the teaching, there are the four truths; by way of the five faculties, there are two truths: the path and cessation.
By means of the origin of identity (*sakkāyasamudaya*), two truths are [established]: suffering and its origin; this is the Mode of Teaching (*desanāhāra*).
In that regard, what is the Investigation (*vicaya*)?
One who does not regard [anything] as "I am this" abandons the three fetters to be abandoned by vision.
This is the investigation.
In this regard, what is the application?
There are three kinds of persons: one who gains knowledge by a condensed statement, one who gains knowledge by an elaborate exposition, and one who is guidable.

One who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññū) has sharp faculties; one who gains knowledge through an elaborated explanation (vipañcitaññū) has duller faculties than that; and one who is led by instruction (neyyo) has duller faculties than those with dull faculties.

Therein, because of his sharp faculties, the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement reaches the plane of vision and attains the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), becoming a "single-seeder" (ekabījako).
This is the first type of stream-enterer.

The one who gains knowledge through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), having reached the plane of vision with weak faculties, attains the fruit of stream-entry and becomes one who goes from family to family;
this is the second type of stream-enterer.
Therein, the one who is guidable (neyya), having reached the plane of vision, attains the fruit of stream-entry and becomes one who has seven births at most.
This is the third stream-enterer.

There is this logical consistency: that by means of weak, medium, or intense faculties, one may realize a weak, medium, or intense plane through the abandoning of the view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), or else abandon the various speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).
This is the logical consistency.
In this context, what is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*)?
Herein, the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is the proximate cause for all wrong views.
A personal body (*sakkāya*) is the proximate cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form is the proximate cause for the view of a personal body.
The five material faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form.
The six sense bases are the proximate cause for the conceit "I am."
In this regard, what is the characteristic?
When two views have been abandoned, therein one view goes toward the abandonment of all modes of view.
One becomes free from passion for both the above and the below, free from passion for all things that cause defilement.
"Those [states] born therefrom in another plane"—thus he sees conditions as they really are.
He grasps the entire dependent origination.
This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇo hāro).
In this regard, what is the fourfold method of analysis (catubyūha-hāra)?
What is the Blessed One’s intention in this sutta?
It is that those beings who will not find delight [in the world] will strive for the abandoning of wrong views.
This is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here.
This is the Fourfold Array method of exposition (*catubyūha-hāra*).
In that regard, what is the Turning Back method of exposition (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*)?
These five faculties that are soft are the five lower fetters.
They eradicate them entirely through the mode of development: faith is the power for the liberation of one in training by way of abandoning covetousness and ill will;
faith is the power by way of views regarding the higher fetters; and the faculty of mindfulness [arises] because of the exertion of the faculty of energy.
Because they have been exerted, they reach the ultimate goal.
In this context, those which are the faculties are the path that abandons defilement;
this is cessation, having the nature of non-arising in the future; this is suffering.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Conversion (Āvaṭṭa-hāra).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Analysis (Vibhatti-hāra)?
One who regards [the self] as "I am this" does so with an excessive worldly basis, and not through noble application; such a person abandons the view of a personal entity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
That which is called "excessive" refers to a particular level [of spiritual attainment].
Therein, one attains excess on that particular level by way of five aspects: through virtue, conduct, erudition, concentration, and the happiness of renunciation.
In this regard, one who perceives themselves as having attained what they have not attained takes up overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
On this very occasion of the arising of the matter, the Blessed One spoke this discourse:
“One who is virtuous merely by way of vows.

In that context, for one who perceives what has not been attained as attained, whatever concentration he possesses is materialistic and cultivated by base persons; for it is worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are called “base persons.”
And whatever mundane concentration there is that arises by resorting to the Noble Path, yet is un-noble—that is the un-noble concentration frequented by base persons.

But he who does not know and does not see according to reality in the manner of the Noble Ones abandons the attainment; whereas he who is led by the Noble concentration—which is not frequented by base persons and is non-material—is led therein. In this context, "base persons" refers to noble individuals.
The concentration frequented by them is "frequented by base persons."
Therefore, one who does not regard [anything] as "this I am" causes that [view] to fall away by means of the one question to be answered with analysis (*vibhajjavyākaraṇīya*).
In this context, what is the turning back (*parivattanā*)?

By means of this stage of vision, the defilements are to be abandoned; even though they were not explicitly specified by the Blessed One, they are to be demonstrated by him as being abandoned by those [means].
In this context, what is the synonym?
That which is the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and the view of a self (attadiṭṭhi)—
this is the plane.

Those defilements which ought to be abandoned are not yet abandoned, even though they have not been specifically designated by the Blessed One as either the view of eternalism (*sassataditthi*) or the view of annihilationism (*ucchedaditthi*). That which is the view of finitude (*pariyantaditthi*) is also the view of eternalism;
that which is the view of infinitude (*apariyantaditthi*) is also the view of eternalism.
The view of annihilationism is the view of nihilism.
The view of eternalism is the view of non-action.
This is a synonym.
In this context, what is description?
Craving is described by way of the description of fetters;
the path is described by way of the description of attainment.
The faculties are described by way of the description of their acquisition.
In this regard, what is the entry point?
The personality-belief (sakkāya) is suffering, and it is to be abandoned through vision.
The origin is the path.
And those faculties have been demonstrated within the aggregates, elements, and bases.
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification?
For that concerning which this discourse was spoken by the Blessed One has been pointed out therein.
In that context, what is the requisite?
Consciousness is both the cause-condition and the causal seed of name-and-form.
Thus, ignorance and volitional formations are the conditions.

The method of cessation is not another way [of explaining] all existence; rather, whatever is the cause of all existence and the condition for external objects is right view. Furthermore, the voice of others and wise attention are the conditions.
That wisdom which brings about [this understanding] is the cause of right view. Right intention arises from it, and that which is right concentration is its requisite.
In this context, what is the application?
It is the non-contemplation [of the self] in the thought "I am this," regarding [the aggregates] as suffering, as a disease, and so forth—
[comprising] fifteen terms.
“Blessed One, what is the purpose of the virtues? What is their benefit?
“Ānanda, the virtues have non-regret as their purpose, up to liberation.
In this regard, there are two kinds of purpose:”
There is the meaning of the person and the meaning of the word.
In this regard, what is the meaning of the person?
That which is the absence of subsequent regret is non-remorse; this is the meaning of the person.
Just as someone who cultivates this purpose and practices it might say: "Something here depends on me; for the sake of that purpose, I am undertaking this action.
This is the meaning of the person (*purisattha*). In this context, what is the meaning of the word (*vacanattha*)?
Virtues that are either bodily or verbal good conduct are "non-remorse.
In this context, there is merely the speaking of virtue and the vow;
the state of having performed the work of a Sugata, which is good conduct, is this non-remorse.
Thus, up to the word "liberation" (vimutti), there are two meanings for each individual term:
the meaning of the person (purisattha) and the meaning of the word (vacanattha). Just as in this sutta, so too in all suttas there are these two meanings.
For this is the ultimate meaning (paramattha) and the supreme meaning (uttamattha).
That which is realized by depending on the realization of Nibbāna, and that which is to be realized for oneself—this is called "the doing of what was to be done.
Furthermore, he understands this synonym.
The meaning of the words is that by means of this, the connected sense is obtained.
In this regard, whatever goal a disciple aspires to,
the attainment of that is the "benefit for man" (*purisattha*).
Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One teaches, the communication of the meaning of each such Dhamma is [the benefit].
This is the meaning: therein, non-remorse regarding the precepts is both the benefit and the advantage.
And this is the advantage—that one does not go to a state of misery.
Just as it was said by the Blessed One: "When the Dhamma is well-practiced, the practitioner of the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery"—this is the meaning.
When a person, with reference to the virtues on the plane of development, is endowed with virtue, and so on up to liberation—thus is the aggregate of virtue.
In that context, both the non-remorse which is indicated by way of underlying tendency and that virtue constitute the aggregate of virtue.
And gladness, rapture, and tranquility, together with the faculty of concentration, constitute the aggregate of concentration.
That which one who is concentrated understands as it truly is—this is the aggregate of wisdom.
These three aggregates are virtue, concentration, and wisdom. In that way he fulfills virtue;
by means of the faculty of energy, for that reason he fulfills virtue, and he exerts effort for the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.

The faculty of energy is defined as follows: for the abandoning of what has arisen, for the arising of the wholesome that has not yet arisen, and for the further increase of the wholesome that has already arisen.
Therein, that which is the aggregate of concentration is the faculty of concentration.
The aggregate of wisdom is the faculty of wisdom; it is to be seen within the four right efforts.
Likewise, that which one exerts oneself for the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen is the first right effort.
That which [one exerts oneself] for [the abandoning of unwholesome states] that have already arisen is the second.
The four right efforts are to be seen within the four jhānas.

Likewise, by means of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the element of renunciation is predominant, as are the three types of thought: thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill-will, and thoughts of non-cruelty;
these are common to all.
The bodily pleasure brought about by the joy of one who loves what is dear—due to the love that is not bound by craving—is happiness.
The non-distraction therein is concentration.
This is the five-factored first jhāna.

That mental tranquility which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought and is opposed to agitation, as well as the defilement and the feverish burning—these are ceased in the first jhāna.
Likewise, both that tranquility of the defilements and that tranquility of applied and sustained thought—both these states are tranquilized herein.
In this context, the pleasure and the state of being pleased of both body and mind is the tranquility of one who possesses rapture and pleasure.
That which is the singleness of mind, and by means of that singleness the internal clarity of mind—this is the fourth factor of jhāna.
Thus, internal clarity, mental singleness, rapture, and bliss: this is the second jhāna, consisting of four factors.

When one whose body is tranquil experiences bliss, having been suffused with that intense bliss, there is a mental bliss; being free from passion for rapture, he thus acquires equanimity through that freedom from passion for rapture.
Thus, with the fading away of rapture, he attains equanimity;
he experiences pleasure and attains mindfulness together with right discernment.
If there is mindfulness and unification of mind, this is the third jhāna with five factors.

That the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated—this is the aspect of penetration belonging to unification of mind. In the first jhāna, although there is one-pointedness of mind, it does not reach full perfection because of the presence of eye-sensation.
Just as in the fourth jhāna, so too that which consists of equanimity, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind—this is the fourth jhāna.
Just as concentration is to be demonstrated, so too is the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) to be seen within the four noble truths.
That which one who is concentrated understands as it truly is—that understanding is fourfold: as foul, as suffering, and as non-self.
Whatever is the object of that [understanding] is the noble truth of suffering. Understanding which, when one understands it, leads to disenchantment and liberation—likewise [is to be seen].

The abandoning of the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance—this is cessation. The arising of the taints on the plane where they have not yet been abandoned is the origin.
These four noble truths are to be seen by means of the faculty of wisdom.
That one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are—this is the plane of vision.
Understanding the fruit of stream-entry as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted; this is "the thinning.

One becomes disenchanted with and detached from sensual desire and ill will, and the fruit of once-returning—this is the stage of development of the first jhāna, the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and the fruit of non-returning.
That which is liberated by means of that liberation is the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance, and the fruit of arahantship.

These states of non-remorse and the faculty of energy constitute the four right endeavors; non-remorse and everything from that point upward as far as concentration constitute the four jhānas and the faculty of concentration. That which one who is concentrated understands as it really is—these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Based upon the fulfillment of virtue, with a mind undisturbed by signs associated with generosity and penetration, this is the faculty of mindfulness; these are the four foundations of mindfulness.

Furthermore, in this teaching of the Dhamma, the faculty of seeing that has been seen in three instances through the abandoning of defilements constitutes the virtue of the trainee (*sekkha-sīla*); this is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
And the four factors of stream-entry are the fruits.
The faculties of concentration (*samādhindriya*), together with their requisites, are to be demonstrated in all the discourses (*sutta*).
The attainment of jhāna through the recollection of knowledge grasped by energy is wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*).
