This is the intended meaning.
In this context, what is the "turning over" (āvaṭṭa)?
By means of that which pertains to defilement, it demonstrates suffering and its origin.
The path partaking of penetration and cessation.
In this regard, what is the analysis?

One born of distress, born of disease, speaks of disease as the self; that is not unilaterally so, for it may be due to lack of attention that one born of distress does not speak of disease as the self.
In this context, what is the method of reversal (*parivattana*)?
It is the reversal of the stages for the purpose of demonstrating the opposing side.
In this context, what is the method of synonyms (*vevacana*)?
One speaks of a disease as the self; one speaks of an arrow as the self.
All fifteen phrases should be stated in this way.
In that regard, what is the description?
"Born of torment" is a designation for the basis of mental distress (*domanassa*).
He designates all [these] by way of verbal designation.
He speaks of "sickness," which is the perversion regarding self; he designates this by way of the designation of defilement (*saṅkilesa*).
That which one does not delight in is suffering; this is designated by way of the designation of the removal of perversion.
Those worlds, being unmade, are designated by way of their diversity through the middle way.
In this regard, what is the entry?

"Born of torment" refers to the three unwholesome roots; these are formations included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Among the elements (*dhātu*), they belong to the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*); among the bases (*āyatana*), they belong to the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*).
Among the faculties (*indriya*), the female faculty and the male faculty are their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
In this context, what is the purification (*sodhana*)?
The beginning of the discourse is pure.
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying the Foundation?
"Fever" refers to those beings in the world who are designated by a designation of unity; they are unmade beings in the world designated by way of diversity through the middle.
In this context, what is the requisite?
"Born of torment" means that improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) is the cause and the perversion (*vipallāsa*) is the condition.
In this regard, one is attached to a self by means of two factors: both the mind (*citta*) and mental states (*cetasika-dhamma*), as one misapprehends them through that perversion.
Another method: the perception of non-self eradicates the perception of self regarding mental phenomena.
This is another method:
the perception of impermanence [is applied] to mental phenomena, but not the perception of self.
"This is called 'mind' (citta), or 'mentality' (mano), or 'consciousness' (viññāṇa); this has long been held to be 'mine,' 'this I am,' 'this is my self.
In that regard, this contemplation of mental states (dhammānupassanā) is also a perception of phenomena (dhammasaññā).
What is its cause, what is its condition?
“I-making” is the cause; “mine-making” is the condition.
In this context, what is the application?
“This world has come into being through torment”—this refers to unwholesome consciousness as the condition for name-and-form, up to aging and death. This is the application.
Thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom: the abandoning of the unwholesome roots.
Therein, the cessation of ignorance, and from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of aging and death—this is the application.
There are four types of persons:
"One who goes with the stream, one who goes against the stream, one established in self, one who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—
he is a brahmin. In this context, he who goes with the stream indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds as long as he pursues those pleasures.
This is the unwholesome root of greed; it is itself craving. One who is carried away by those sensual pleasures is said to be "going with the stream.
Whatever person, being led by them, on that account and for that reason, performs unwholesome action by way of body and speech—this is called "one who performs evil karma.
For such a person, there are three streams: personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
Through these three doors, one arises in the threefold realm: in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu).
By contrast, it is one who does not indulge in sensual pleasures and who does not cling to precepts and vows.
He who, through the abandoning of the view of a personal body, sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it truly is;
and by means of which he practices those teachings;
and on account of which he stands [as one]—he, it is said, is a brahmin, an Arahant.
In this context, the Arahant has gone to the further shore; for one who has gone to the further shore, he stands on dry land in the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining.
"Flowing with the stream" refers to the non-abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned by vision.

"Flowing against the stream" refers to the abandonment of those defilements that are to be abandoned by the fruit [of the path], and by the term "steadfastness," it refers to the abandonment of the five lower fetters.
In this context, he speaks of the path by means of "one who goes with the stream.
He speaks of the path by means of "one who goes against the stream" and "one who is established.
By "one who has gone to the further shore," the disciples, the adepts, and the perfectly enlightened Buddhas are described.
By "one who goes with the stream," he refers to the practice leading to the origination of identity (*sakkāya*).
By "one who goes against the stream" and by "one who is established," he refers to the practice leading to the cessation of identity.
By "one who has gone to the further shore," the ten qualities of the arahant who is beyond training (*asekha*) are stated.
This is the meaning of the discourse.
In that regard, what is the teaching?
For in this discourse, the four noble truths are taught.
And the transcending of the world of the three realms.
In this context, what is the method of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*)?

It is the inquiry: "He who indulges in sensual pleasures might commit evil; he who does not indulge in sensual pleasures would not commit evil deeds"; and [the inquiry]: "He who has crossed over from these two planes and reached the further shore. This inquiry is the method of investigation.
"Reasoning" (*yutti*) refers to that which is consistent with the suttas and not inconsistent; this is reasoning.
"Footing" (*padaṭṭhāna*) refers to the footing for the seven fetters for one who goes with the stream.
Unwholesome action is the footing for the roots of the unwholesome.
Going against the stream is the proximate cause for seeing things as they truly are.
Being established is the proximate cause for being unshakable.
Having gone to the further shore is sometimes the proximate cause for the [spiritual] plane.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics?
It is that which goes with the stream by way of craving;
it goes by way of all the defilements.
He who strives against the stream:
he strives against the stream of all defilements, including craving.
He who is established by himself is established in body, and he is also established in speech and mind.
This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra).
In that regard, what is the Fourfold Array (catubyūha)?
Here, in this discourse, what is the Blessed One’s intention?
"Those who will not delight in the practice that goes with the stream will strive against the stream"—this is the intended meaning as far as the "ground" (bhūmi).
"The Conversion" (āvaṭṭa): four suttas are taught here in this discourse.
In that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Analysis (vibhatti-hāra)?
He who indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds is one who goes with the stream;
for even a stream-enterer does not categorically indulge in sensual pleasures,
nor does he perform such evil deeds as would lead to that state.
Even though a trainee (*sekha*) might commit an evil deed as specified in the Sutta, he does not go with the stream; this is a question to be answered by analysis (*vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya*).
He neither indulges in sensual pleasures nor performs evil deeds and goes against the stream;

yet, it is not the case that all outsiders (*bāhiraka*) who are free from lust for sensual pleasures do not indulge in sensual pleasures while nevertheless performing evil deeds and going with the stream. This is the analysis.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Reversal?
It is the opposite of what has been demonstrated.

As for synonyms: regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*), there are both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*); and as for possessions, these include forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, as well as sons, wives, slaves, laborers, and servants.
"Designation" means that all worldlings are designated by way of unity.
"One who goes with the stream" is designated by way of the manifestation of defilements.
But those persons who are trainees are designated by way of Nibbāna.
But those who are non-returners (anāgāmī) are designated by way of an irremovable designation; this is the designation.
As for the "entry": he who goes with the stream is suffering;
those factors belonging to him are the origin of suffering.

Whatever is form, this is the aggregate of form; thus all five aggregates are dependent origination. Those defilements included within the aggregate of formations are the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), and they are designated among the faculties.
Regarding "purification": whatever undertaking this discourse was taught for, that entire undertaking is pure.

Regarding "the foundation": by means of one who goes against the stream, all stream-enterers are indicated as a single unity; those in training who go against the stream of the underlying tendency to lust, as well as the path and the person in training, are established as "steadfast."
One who is free from passion is designated by way of unity.
"One who has gone to the further shore" refers to all Arahants, all Paccekabuddhas, and all Sammasambuddhas, who are designated by way of unity.
"Requisite" refers to the condition of evil friends for one going with the stream, and the obsession with sensual pleasures as its cause.

There are two causes and two conditions for one who goes against the stream, leading up to the arising of right view. For such a person, the path already attained is the cause, the undertaking is the condition, and there is both a bodily and a mental component.
This is the analysis; however, there is no ground for a formal synthesis (*samāropanā*) of this sutta.
The five benefits for those who have followed the stream and have thoroughly penetrated the teachings up to right view should be set forth in detail according to the sutta.
While he is practicing, striving, and exerting himself, he becomes ill at the time of death; having become a deity, he attains *paccekabodhi*.
"Entered through the ear" means it was accomplished by hearing the true Dhamma.
Yet his mind is not parched for higher wisdom and insight into phenomena, nor is there any lack of penetration.
And this discourse was taught for five types of persons: for the follower by faith with dull faculties and with keen faculties;
and for the follower of Dhamma with keen faculties and with dull faculties.

However, as for the person of deluded temperament who is unable to apply himself, strive, or exert himself, [the Buddha] shows him the fruit at that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, according to his actual state and his concentration.
It is good that another person declines and is tormented by that [decline], for it does not result in a pleasant ripening.
And for that person, there is [kamma] to be experienced either in this very life, upon rebirth, or in subsequent lives.
In this regard, if a person who follows the Dhamma (dhammānusārī) has acquired the teachings through hearing, he attains [the goal] by applying himself.
The follower by Dhamma with dull faculties reaches [the goal] while ill.
The follower by faith with sharp faculties reaches [the goal] at the time of death.
The one with dull faculties, having become a deva, reaches [the goal].
When one who has become a deva does not attain [the goal], he does not, by that very passion for the Dhamma or that delight in the Dhamma, attain *paccekabodhi*.
But he who applies himself, exerts himself, and strives regarding those things that have entered the ear perceives a distinction from what was previously attained; perceiving it, he attains it.
Furthermore, if there is attention toward one who is ill, he attains it by applying himself therein.
If, however, he is filled with a sense of spiritual urgency at the time of death, he attains [the goal] by applying himself there.
But if no such urgency arises for him anywhere, then while he has become a happy deva, his feet—which are now composed of Dhamma—lament thus.
He recognizes: "This is that Dhamma and Discipline wherein we formerly, when we were human beings, practiced the holy life."
Then, having become a deity, he attains [the divine state].
Or, being attached to the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure and dwelling in negligence, he attains *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) by means of that root of merit.
That which is well-mastered through the voice of another and through speech is wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*).
Those phenomena that have been examined by the mind constitute wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*).
That which has been thoroughly penetrated through right view constitutes wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*).
That which has entered the stream and been mastered through speech, such that one attains final nibbāna in this very life—this is the person who is an *arhat*.
One who is reborn as a deity and attains final nibbāna there is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
One who, by means of that root of merit, attains *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) is a person produced from the equipment of prior practice (*pubbayoga-sambhāra-sambhūta*).
"Dhammas entered through the ear" refers to the first basis of liberation; "perfected by speech" refers to the second and third.
The basis of liberation as "reviewed with the mind" is the fourth basis of liberation; "thoroughly penetrated by view" is the fifth basis of liberation.
Regarding the liberation that has entered the ear, it is the speech thoroughly penetrated by verbal expression after having heard the gradual Dhamma with the ear.
He fulfills the aggregate of virtue; when examined by the mind, he fulfills the aggregate of concentration;
when well-penetrated through right view, he fulfills the aggregate of wisdom.
"The teachings entered through hearing become well-learned"—this should be elaborated in detail.

"This is the first manifestation of faith: 'It has been examined by the mind,'" thus he dwells frequently in seclusion; this should be elaborated in detail. "This is the second manifestation of faith:
'It has been well-penetrated by view,'" thus he understands: "There is no further state of being beyond this taintless liberation of mind.
This is the third manifestation of faith.
"States followed by hearing"—this the Teacher shows as the state of training (the *sekha*).
"Examined with the mind"—this the Teacher shows as *arahantship*.
"Thoroughly penetrated by view"—this the Teacher shows as the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"States followed by hearing" shows the escape from sensual pleasures.
"Examined with the mind" shows the escape from the realm of form.
"Thoroughly penetrated by view" shows the escape from the three realms.
This is the meaning of the discourse.
In this regard, what is the "mode of teaching"?
In this sutta, three searches (*esanā*) are taught by means of phenomena that have entered the ear and been mastered through speech: the path of serenity regarding the search for sensual pleasures.
The path of serenity is for one who has well-penetrated views through the search for the holy life.
"Investigation" means that by attending to the discourses and investigating them, one acquires wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī-paññā*).
And as to how one attends to them: it is by means of that [investigation] that one acquires wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-paññā*) regarding the teachings as they have been heard.
When one attends to the Dhamma in this very life, one then acquires wisdom consisting in development;
this is investigation.
Through what has been heard, one acquires wisdom consisting in learning.
Through reflection, one obtains wisdom consisting in reflection; through cultivation, one obtains wisdom consisting in cultivation.
This is the logical connection (*yutti*).
As for the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*): "the teachings followed by the ear" is the proximate cause for hearing the Dhamma.
"Thoroughly mastered by speech" is the proximate cause for one who is applying himself [to meditation].
"Examined with the mind" is the proximate cause for insight (vipassanā) that accords with the Dhamma.
"Examined by view" means examined both by wisdom and examined by right view.
Regarding the "Fourfold Array" (*catubyūha*): what is the Blessed One’s intention in this sutta?
Those who are endowed with these two kinds of wisdom...

[he says] "he has attained extinction" (*sa nibbuto*) to mean the path and fruit, as well as the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*); he means by "giving" (*dāna*) the abandoning of gross defilements.

Through virtue he counsels those of middle standing; through wisdom, he counsels those with subtle defilements. "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this is the ground that has been established.
"Merit increases for one who gives;
enmity does not accumulate for one who is self-restrained."
"The skillful one abandons evil" refers to the Path.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" speaks of the fruit of the Path.
"Merit increases for the one who gives, for the one who restrains himself"—by these three phrases, mundane wholesome roots are described.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this refers to the supramundane wholesome root.
"Merit increases for one who gives; by restraint, enmity is not accumulated"—this indicates the plane of the worldling (*puthujjana*).
"And the skillful one abandons evil"—this indicates the plane of the trainee (*sekkha*).
“Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished”—this refers to the stage of one beyond training (asekkha-bhūmi).
“Merit increases for the giver; by restraint, enmity is not accumulated”—this refers to the practice leading to the path (magganiyā paṭipadā).
“The skillful man abandons evil”—this is the liberation of one in training (sekkha-vimutti).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this is the liberation of one beyond training (*asekkha-vimutti*).

"Merit increases for the giver; by self-restraint, enmity is not accumulated"—this refers to the teaching on generosity, the teaching on virtue, the teaching on the path, and the instruction on worldly phenomena.
"The skillful man abandons evil"—this is the contemplation of the danger (*ādīnava*) in the world.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this has been penetrated even through the Dhamma teaching of self-exaltation.
"Merit increases for one who gives"—by the gift of fearlessness to living beings, he grants fearlessness to those beings through abstention from taking life.
In this way, all the training rules (sikkhāpada) are to be practiced.
"By restraint, enmity is not accumulated": having established oneself in virtue, one restrains the mind; through that restraint, it reaches fulfillment.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished": this refers to the two liberations.
This is the exposition of the sutta.
In this regard, what is the teaching?
What is taught in this sutta?
Two happy destinies: gods and humans, and the fivefold divine sensual pleasures as well as those of humans.
The exposition is by means of two phrases.
"Merit increases for one who gives; enmity does not accumulate for one who is self-restrained; and the skillful one abandons evil"—this states the path.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this teaches the two elements of Nibbāna: that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining.
This is the teaching (*desanā*).

As for the investigation (*vicaya*): by the first phrase, "Merit increases for one who gives," the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of giving (*dānamayika-puññakiriyavatthu*) is stated.
By that, [the merit] of those wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) that are immediate (*ānantariya*) is indicated.
By the second phrase... "it leads," meaning the Dispensation is leading [to liberation]; this is the intended meaning.
By means of non-hearing, non-attention, and non-penetration, the practice leading to the origin of identity is described.
By means of hearing, attention, and penetration, the practice leading to the cessation of identity is described.
This is the turning.
As for "analysis," it is to be answered categorically;
there is no ground for analysis therein.
Reversal (*parivattanā*): Those five benefits are attained in this very life through their fivefold opposite; that is another method regarding those who are being reborn. Synonym (*vevacana*):
"Dhammas entered through the ear" refers to that discourse which is seen, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) which is made known, and that which is well-penetrated and clarified by view.
Description (*paññatti*): "Dhammas entered through the ear" is a teaching described by way of the description of ignorance (*avijjā*).
Attention is described by way of the description of gladness; the benefits pertaining to the present life are also described by way of the description of benefits.

As for the "entry": there are three kinds of wisdom—wisdom consisting of what is heard regarding those things collected by speech, wisdom consisting of reflection regarding those things examined by the mind, and wisdom consisting of cultivation regarding those things well-penetrated by view.

These Noble Truths, the Faculties, the Arising of Knowledge, the Cessation of Ignorance, and Dependent Origination are included among the faculties as three faculties, among the bases as included in the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), and among the elements as included in the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
"Clearing away" refers to the undertaking; "entry into the sutta" is thus established.

"Resolution" refers to the five benefits; these benefits are taught according to their diversity, and the noble terminology is established according to that diversity. Furthermore, "hearing the Dhamma" is taught as a unity.
"Requisite" means that attending upon [the teacher] is the condition for hearing the Dhamma, while faith is the cause.

"Examined with the mind" means that experiencing the meaning is the condition (*paccaya*) and experiencing the Dhamma is the cause (*hetu*). "Well-penetrated by view" means that hearing the true Dhamma and mental attention are the condition, while wisdom consisting of what is heard and wisdom consisting of reflection are the cause.
As for the application: the analyzed discourse is another method; there is no arising apart from the powers.
In this regard, the application constitutes the ground.
In this regard, what is the discourse pertaining to both purification by habituation and penetration?
It is the verse beginning: "For one who gives, merit increases.
Here, "giving" refers to the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of giving.
"By self-restraint, enmity is not accumulated" refers to the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of virtue (*sīlamayika-puññakiriyavatthu*).
"And the skillful one abandons evil" speaks of the abandoning of greed, delusion, and ill-will (*byāpāda*).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" speaks of the removal of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) for greed, delusion, and ill-will.
In the verse "Merit increases for one who gives," non-greed (*alobha*) is the root of the wholesome.
In "By restraint, enmity is not accumulated," non-hatred (*adosa*) is the root of the wholesome.
By the words "By restraint, enmity is not accumulated," one is always free from enmity, free from adversaries, and free from ill will through non-malice.
"The skillful one abandons evil": this is the cessation of ignorance through the arising of knowledge.

By the fourth phrase, through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, there is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust; through the destruction of delusion, there is the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance—this is the investigation (*vicaya*).
As for the application (*yutti*): established in giving, one indeed fulfills both.
One abandons stinginess and merit increases;
this is the logical consistency.
“Foundation” (padaṭṭhāna) means: “Merit increases for one who gives”—this is the foundation for the foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna).

“By restraint, enmity is not accumulated”—this is the foundation for the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna). “And the skillful one abandons evil”—this is the foundation for the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna).
“Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished”—this is the foundation for the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna).
This is the proximate cause.
In this regard, what is the characteristic?
"Merit increases for one who gives; enmity does not accumulate for one who is self-restrained."
Even when returning harm, the skillful person does not act with enmity; rather, through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he abandons evil and is extinguished (nibbuto).

Through the destruction of form and the destruction of feeling—by means of whatever form is seen, the Tathāgata, in describing it, would describe it as the destruction, fading away, and cessation of form—thus [it is] with the five aggregates.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here with the *Catubbyūha* (The Fourfold Array)?
Those who will aspire to great wealth will give gifts for the sake of removing dangers;
those who desire freedom from enmity will abandon the five kinds of enmity; and those who desire what is wholesome will cultivate the Eightfold Path for the sake of abandoning the eight wrongnesses.
"The Blessed One’s intention is this: those who desire to attain Nibbāna will abandon lust, hatred, and delusion.

"Turning back" (*āvatta*) refers to the fact that stinginess in one who does not give, enmity in one who lacks self-restraint, and the non-abandonment of unwholesome evil—these are descriptions of suffering (*dukkha*), not its origin (*samudaya*).
Through non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—these are the three roots of the wholesome (*kusala-mūla*).
The condition for these is the eight rightnesses; this is the path.
Through the destruction of those [defilements of] lust, hatred, and delusion, this is cessation.
As for the analysis: it is not the case that merit increases for one who gives out of fear of royal punishment; and as for one who...
If one gives to those possessed of virtue by means of the consumption of what is unallowable, their merit does not increase.
Thus, if one gives this gift with an unwholesome mind, it increases demerit consisting of the giving of sticks and the giving of weapons, not merit.

Regarding the statement, "From self-restraint, enmity is not accumulated," why is it not absolute? It is because one perceives a certain condition pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), such as: "If kings were to seize me and cut off my hand... and so forth.
One does not create enmity through that restraint.
But he who undertakes it thus—[realizing] that the maturation of the taking of life is evil—refrains from all unwholesome states by way of their cause, both in this very life and in the future.
Through this restraint, enmity is not accumulated.
"Reversal" means: for one who gives, merit increases; for one who does not give, merit does not increase.
That which consists of giving: through self-restraint, enmity is not accumulated; through lack of self-restraint, enmity is produced.
The skillful person abandons evil, but the unskillful person does not abandon it.

Thinking, "He has attained final peace through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion; I shall not summon him by sending a messenger or sending fine gifts, but rather he himself, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, has arrived at our dwelling place.
We have had this Santhāgāra hall constructed; let us bring the One of Ten Powers here and have him recite auspicious verses," they approached him.
“They approached the assembly hall” means that on that day, having completed the decorative painting in the assembly hall, the builders were just about to leave.

Thinking, “The Buddhas are by nature inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest; they might stay in the village or not,” they approached the Blessed One with the intention, “We shall attend to it only after ascertaining the Blessed One’s mind.
But now, having ascertained his mind and wishing to attend to it, they approached the assembly hall.
"Sabbasanthariṃ" means that they approached the Blessed One in such a way that everything was completely spread out.
In this context, those Malla kings, having attended to the assembly hall, had the city streets swept, hoisted banners, and set up golden water-jars and plantain trees;
they then adorned the entire city with garlands of lamps so that it resembled a sky filled with stars.
Having made it so, they had milk given to the children who were being nursed, and they fed and laid the young boys down very quickly.
"Make no loud noise; today the Teacher will dwell within the village itself, for Buddhas indeed desire little sound," they proclaimed by means of a drum.
Then, taking their own torches and sticks, they approached the Blessed One.
"Having placed the Blessed One at their head" means having made the Blessed One their leader; there, seated in the midst of the monks and lay followers, the Blessed One shone exceedingly.
He was serene on all sides, golden-hued, beautiful, and lovely to behold. From his front body, a golden ray arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky.
From his back body, from his right hand, from his left hand, and from the soles of his feet, a golden ray [and a coral-colored ray] [arose].
Having arisen, it occupies a space of eighty cubits upon the solid earth; likewise,
the six-colored rays of a Buddha’s radiance flash, shimmer, and stream forth for a distance of eighty cubits all around,
such that all directions appear as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, like streams of molten gold pouring from a golden vessel.
As if being sprinkled with water, as if draped in a spread golden cloth, and as if strewn with the pollen of *kiṃsuka*, *kiṃsukāraka*,
and *kaṇikāra* flowers stirred up by the *verambha* wind, his body— resplendent with the eighty minor marks and the radiance of a fathom-wide aura,
and shining with the thirty-two supreme major marks— appeared like the vault of heaven with its stars risen, like a forest of lotuses in full bloom, or like a tree covered in every kind of flower.

The Pāricchattaka tree, one hundred *yojanas* in height, is extinguished by thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs (*cakkavattī*), thirty-two kings of the gods, and thirty-two Great Brahmās;
but for the one beyond training (*asekkha*), there is no such extinction. Regarding synonyms:
merit increases for the one who gives, and merit also increases for the one who rejoices in the gift.
Merit increases both for one who concentrates the mind and for one who performs services. Regarding the "proclamation":
"Merit increases for the giver" is proclaimed by way of the proclamation of the destruction of the basis for non-greed.

"By restraint, enmity is not accumulated" is proclaimed by way of the proclamation of the destruction of the basis for non-hate. "And the wise man abandons evil" is proclaimed by way of the proclamation of the destruction of the basis for non-delusion.
"Entry" refers to the five faculties: merit increases for one who gives; enmity does not accumulate for one who restrains himself; through restraint comes the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).

Restraint regarding the six faculties is the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). That which the skillful person abandons—the evil—is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*). "He is extinguished through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion" is the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*).
Among the elements, it is the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*); among the bases, it is the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
Regarding "purification": the undertaking by which this discourse was taught is pure.
The "foundation" is giving; it is described as a unity.
Generosity, relinquishment—the gift of Dhamma and the gift of material goods—the eight types of giving should be explained in detail; this constitutes diversity.
It is not described by means of a description of unity regarding the one who gives.
It is described by means of a description of forbearance as blameless.
It is described by means of a description of the energy of restraint: "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished."
"Requisites": for giving, joy is the condition and non-greed is the cause.
For self-restraint, wise attention is the cause and relinquishment is the condition.
Regarding "the skillful one abandons evil," seeing things as they truly are is the condition and the acquisition of knowledge is the cause.
"The destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion—that is Nibbāna": this external report, internal wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), the path, the cause, and the condition [for Nibbāna].
As for the application (*samāropana*): from the verse "Merit increases for one who gives," it follows that his virtue (*sīla*) also increases, and his self-restraint (*saṃyama*) also increases.
"By self-restraint, enmity is not accumulated.
Other defilements are also not accumulated—those taints (*āsava*) and vexations (*vighāta*) that might arise because of them do not arise for him either.

"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished": through the destruction of lust and hatred, and through the destruction of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) to lust, as well as of hatred and delusion, he is extinguished; this refers to both the *nibbāna*-element with residue remaining and the *nibbāna*-element without residue remaining.
This is the coordination.
